neighbours.label: ' who' / ' would' in a non-restrictive 'X, who would hardly / never ...' clause arguing from what a kind of person would typically do
fire: The damage does not look like the work of vandals, who would hardly have swept up the glass.
This letter cannot have come from a lawyer, who would never make such a careless mistake.
The tracks were not left by wolves, who would hardly walk so close to the fire.
It was clearly not written by a native speaker, who would never confuse those two words.
The fire was not started by campers, who would hardly choose such a steep slope.
This cannot be the camp of soldiers, who would never leave their rifles in the rain.
The graves were not dug by looters, who would hardly have put the stones back.
The note did not come from a doctor, who would never recommend such a dose.
quiet: The damage does not look like the work of vandals, and the glass was swept up.
This letter came from a lawyer, and it contains a careless mistake.
The tracks were left by wolves that walked close to the fire.
It was clearly written by a native speaker in a great hurry.
The fire was started by campers on a steep slope.
This is the camp of soldiers, and their rifles are out in the rain.
The graves were dug by looters and the stones were put back.
The note came from a doctor and recommends a small dose.

notes: Card: top example 'not indicative of barbarian activity, who ⟦would⟧ hardly be mindful to'; others are verbs/commas inside generic if-clauses ('If an alcoholic ⟦has⟧', 'If an animal ⟦is⟧'). Probes: fresh if-clauses did not fire (0.02-0.07); ', who would hardly bother' 0.80, ', who would never have left' 0.59; 'A professional thief would hardly' 0.18; ', who could scarcely' 0.07. The label covers only the construction that fired; the if-clause part of the pole is unexplained.
